message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different kinds of workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Specialized for parallel numeric work – originally for rendering graphics, now also used for scientific, machine‑learning, and other compute‑heavy tasks. |
| **Architecture** | Few cores (typically 2–32), each very powerful with deep pipelines, sophisticated branch prediction, large caches, and complex control logic. | Hundreds or thousands of simpler cores arranged in SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) groups; each core is lightweight and optimized for throughput rather than latency. |
| **Instruction Set** | Complex, rich set of instructions, including many that handle branching, memory management, and I/O. | Simpler instruction set focused on arithmetic and data movement; less emphasis on branching. |
| **Execution Model** | Mostly serial or lightly parallel; can execute one instruction per cycle per core. | Highly parallel; can execute the same instruction on many data elements simultaneously (SIMD). |
| **Memory Hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, sophisticated cache coherence protocols, support for virtual memory. | Smaller per‑core caches, often shared memory pools, less sophisticated coherence; relies on high bandwidth memory (HBM, GDDR). |
| **Latency vs Throughput** | Optimized for low latency – quick response to individual requests. | Optimized for high throughput – many operations completed per second, even if each takes longer. |
| **Typical Workloads** | Control flow heavy tasks: OS kernel, web servers, database engines, general software. | Data‑parallel tasks: image/video processing, physics simulations, AI/ML inference/training, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Power Efficiency** | More power per core due to complexity; balanced for performance and energy. | Very power‑efficient per operation when running at scale; can consume a lot of power overall when fully utilized. |

In short, CPUs excel at handling diverse, irregular tasks quickly, while GPUs shine when you have a massive amount of similar calculations that can run in lockstep. That’s why modern systems often combine both: the CPU orchestrates the program, and the GPU accelerates the heavy numeric parts.
